newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic's party digs in heels on election dispute.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic's party digs in heels on election dispute.

text.p: Signs that Serbia's ruling Socialists will resist wholesale concessions on disputed election results increased on Sunday with allegations of opposition "terrorism" and a telling snub at a state funeral.

In another hint of hardening lines, a senior minister who had earlier tacitly conceded official wrongdoing said an electoral commission ruling that upheld an opposition victory in Belgrade was a "nightmare of legal nonsense".

Supporters of the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition have staged nine weeks of peaceful mass demonstrations against the Socialists' annulment of Serbia-wide municipal elections it claimed to have won.

An OSCE investigation dismissed the Socialists' claim of unspecified "irregularities" in the balloting and verified that Zajedno captured majorities in 14 major Serbian towns including the two biggest, Belgrade and Nis.

With the West warning President Slobodan Milosevic to respect democratic principles or forget about aid for Serbia's wrecked economy, Socialist-led electoral commissions admitted Zajedno victories in Belgrade and Nis last week.

Hardline Socialists lodged an appeal against the commission verdict in Nis but it was swiftly rejected by the municipal court. Heartened Zajedno activists said they would convene the new local assembly on January 27 as a result.
But the Socialists retained other avenues for legalistic obstruction and political sabotage through state-dominated higher courts and the mainstream media, analysts said.
They believe Milosevic is playing for time by withholding clear instructions, giving hardliners free rein to manoeuvre to regain political advantage.

Renewed anti-Serb violence in the Albanian-majority province of Kosovo could be an opportunity for Milosevic to divert attention from the election problem and reassert the appeal of strong Socialist leadership.

State-run mainstream media jumped on allegations by the Serb Socialist mayor of Pristina in Kosovo that Zajedno was involved in a car bombing that gravely injured the Serb rector of the city's university last week.

"(Pristina Mayor Dusan) Simic said Albanian extremists and separatists, who before the international community act as peacemakers, (as well as) democrats and opposition demonstrators in Serbia, stand here behind the darkest political terrorism and ethnic cleansing (of Serbs)," the official Yugoslav Tanjug news agency reported.

In Belgrade, Zajedno condemned the bomb attack and denied any connection with it. "Whoever committed this shameless action committed it against the democratisation of Serbia and against the interests of all citizens of Serbia," it said.

Another indication of hardline sentiment in the Socialist Party (SPS) was the absence of Yugoslav Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic from the weekend funeral of his counterpart in Montenegro, Serbia's tiny federal partner.

Belgrade sent only a junior foreign ministry official to the memorial rites for Janko Jeknic, an eminent career diplomat who helped tiny Montenegro pursue pro-Western economic and political policies. He died in a car crash on Friday.
Analysts said the snub reflected Belgrade's anger at Montenegrin calls for an election compromise with Zajedno.
In contrast with Serbia, Montenegro has pursued free market reforms and believes the power of Serbian leftists must wane if it is to gain access to vital Western investment.

A third signal that diehards were gaining the upper hand over pro-concession moderates in ruling circles was a retreat by deputy Serbian premier Ratko Markovic from a statement he made on January 11 that "genuine and complete" election results must be honoured in Serbia.
On Saturday, Markovic said electoral commissioners' subsequent decision to recognise Zajedno's victory in Belgrade was a "nightmare of legal nonsense, unlawfulness and error".
He said the commission was not competent to overturn prior court decisions, which favoured the SPS. The deadline for the SPS to appeal against the Belgrade ruling was Monday.
Zajedno planned its 63rd straight day of often festive and witty demonstrations by urging faithful to take their pets for a walk in Belgrade on Sunday to challenge riot police cordons.

But daily rallies notwithstanding, Serbia's crisis looked set to drag on without resolution barring strikes in support of Zajedno by traditionally pro-Socialist workers and farmers who have shunned the protest movement so far.
